item.text: {"text":"Recent evidence supports testing negative sampling while retaining HSTU, but does not establish that harder negatives improve this benchmark. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compares random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling: results depend on dataset popularity structure; random sampling favors head items, while popularity-based alternatives can improve balance at an overall accuracy cost. [CATS (2026)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) motivates sampling from neighboring item clusters rather than concentrating on the positive’s own cluster, where false negatives may accumulate. This supports moderate semantic neighbors as an experimental hypothesis, not treating title similarity as verified negative feedback.\n\nSampling correction needs an explicit objective and proposal distribution. [Correcting the LogQ Correction (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) highlights that the positive is always included, unlike sampled negatives; applying the same correction indiscriminately is inappropriate. [NeurIPS 2025 theory](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/42b7c2f6d320d1fe1afa899a6319d6d7-Abstract-Conference.html) also establishes limits on unbiased softmax estimation from sampled subsets. A practical experiment: compare uniform multi-negative softmax against a gradual uniform/moderate-neighbor mixture; exclude known training positives and padding, retain uniform support, and calculate proposal probabilities after filtering if approximating full-catalog softmax. Unknown false negatives remain unidentifiable. Keep one trained HSTU per category; select using the fixed host macro validation HR@10, since training margins alone cannot establish ranking gains."}
